frames.narration: A user opens a Google service. DNS has given the browser a VIP, a virtual address that belongs to the service and not to any machine, and the browser sends its first packet (a TCP SYN) to it. The packet arrives at the cluster's router.
Every Maglev machine in the cluster announces the same VIP at the same cost, so the router uses ECMP and spreads packets over them by a hash of the connection. This one goes to Maglev machine 1.

states.m1: packet received straight from the card

frames.narration: Machine 1 matches the packet to the VIP and finds no entry for this 5-tuple in its connection table. It hashes the 5-tuple to a slot of the lookup table, which says which backend owns that slot, and records the choice in the connection table.

messages.label: GRE-wrapped packet to the chosen backend

frames.narration: The backend replies with the VIP as its source address, directly to the router and the user. The larger response packets never pass through Maglev, which the paper calls Direct Server Return.

Now Maglev machine 1 is taken down for an upgrade, and the router starts sending this connection's packets to machine 2, which has no entry for it. This is the case where per-machine tracking is not enough.

Machine 2 uses the lookup table. Every Maglev machine builds it the same way from the same backend pool, so the same hash lands in the same slot and on the same backend. The connection carries on without the user noticing.

messages.label: same backend, from the lookup table

frames.narration: Later one backend fails its health check. The controller takes it out of the pool and the machines rebuild their tables. Because of Maglev hashing, the slots of the other backends mostly stay as they were, so only connections on the failed backend, plus a few more, are affected.
